marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q001.takeaway: Interstitial cells of Cajal generate gastrointestinal slow waves and couple electrical activity to smooth muscle.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q001.displayText:
Interstitial cells of Cajal generate gastrointestinal slow waves and couple electrical activity to smooth muscle.

The interstitial cells of Cajal undergo cyclic changes in membrane potential due to unique ion channels that periodically open and produce inward (pacemaker) currents that generate slow-wave activity.

Interstitial cells of Cajal are the pacemaker cells of the GIT that initiate the basic electrical rhythm (BER). These are stellate mesenchymal pacemaker cells with smooth muscle-like features.

In the stomach and the small intestine, these cells are located in the circular smooth muscle layer near the myenteric plexus. In the colon, they are at the submucosal border of the circular muscle layer.

The slow waves usually do not by themselves cause muscle contraction in most parts of the gastrointestinal tract, except perhaps in the stomach. Instead, they mainly excite the appearance of intermittent spike potentials, and the spike potentials in turn actually excite the muscle contraction.

Note: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal.
emphasis: Interstitial cells of Cajal generate gastrointestinal slow waves and couple electrical activity to smooth muscle

rationales.a: Myenteric neurons modulate motility but do not generate the basic slow waves.
rationales.b: Smooth muscle responds to slow waves; ICC are the pacemaker cells.
rationales.d: Parasympathetic neurons modulate excitability rather than generating the intrinsic slow-wave rhythm.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q002.takeaway: Slow-wave frequency is lowest in the stomach, increases through small intestine and is highest in duodenum.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q002.displayText:
Slow-wave frequency is lowest in the stomach, increases through small intestine and is highest in duodenum.

Among the given options, the least frequency of slow waves is seen in the stomach (4/min).

The Basal electrical rhythm (BER), also called slow-wave, is a rhythmic fluctuation of membrane potential in the gastrointestinal smooth muscle. It is initiated by the interstitial cells of Cajal. The membrane potential fluctuates between -65 mV and -45 mV.

The BER is seen in all sites of gastrointestinal smooth muscle except in the esophagus and proximal stomach.

The rate of BER in various sites is as follows:
• Stomach: 4/min
• Duodenum: 12/min
• Distal ileum: 8/min
• Cecum: 2/min
• Sigmoid colon: 6/min

The BER does not cause contraction of the smooth muscle. However, when the BER is superimposed by the spike potentials, it increases muscle tension.

Acetylcholine causes an increase in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension. Epinephrine causes a decrease in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension.

Muscle contraction can occur only when the motor stimulus is provided during the depolarisation part of the BER.

Thus, BER does not cause muscle contraction by itself, but controls the rate and organization sites of the muscle contractions, as in coordination of the peristaltic activity and setting the rhythm of segmentation.
emphasis: Slow-wave frequency is lowest in the stomach, increases through small intestine and is highest in duodenum

rationales.a: Duodenum has the fastest small-intestinal slow-wave frequency.
rationales.b: Ileal frequency is higher than gastric frequency.
rationales.c: Jejunum slow waves occur more often than gastric waves.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q003.takeaway: Slow-wave frequency rises along the small intestine and is greatest in the ileum among these choices.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q003.displayText:
Slow-wave frequency rises along the small intestine and is greatest in the ileum among these choices.

Among the given options, the frequency of 'slow waves' is maximum in the ileum (8/min).

Normal intestinal motility is determined by two patterns of electrical activity - slow waves and spike potentials.

Slow waves, also known as basic electrical rhythm, are partial depolarizations of smooth muscle cells, spreading along the GIT. They originate from the interstitial cells of Cajal. The smooth muscles are in a hyperpolarized state, having a resting membrane potential of -50 to -60 mV.

These waves are not action potentials themselves and they do not cause any contractions. Slow waves raise the membrane potential by 5-15 mV, bringing it closer to the threshold enabling spike potential (true action potential) to occur. Therefore, they set the basic rhythm of GIT.
emphasis: Slow-wave frequency rises along the small intestine and is greatest in the ileum among these choices

rationales.a: Stomach slow waves are slower than small-intestinal frequencies.
rationales.c: Colon has its own slower patterns and is not the maximum in this comparison.
rationales.d: Rectal activity is not faster than ileal slow waves.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q004.takeaway: The facial nerve is not the afferent limb of the swallowing reflex; glossopharyngeal and vagus carry major sensory input.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q004.displayText:
The facial nerve is not the afferent limb of the swallowing reflex; glossopharyngeal and vagus carry major sensory input.

The facial nerve is a part of an efferent limb (and not afferent) of the swallowing reflex.
emphasis: The facial nerve is not the afferent limb of the swallowing reflex; glossopharyngeal and vagus carry major sensory input

rationales.a: Trigeminal sensory fibers contribute oral/tactile afferent information.
rationales.c: Glossopharyngeal afferents from oropharynx are important in triggering swallowing.
rationales.d: Vagal afferents carry sensory information from pharynx/larynx.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q005.takeaway: Peristaltic contractions propel chyme aborally through the small intestine.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q005.displayText:
Peristaltic contractions propel chyme aborally through the small intestine.

Chyme is propelled forward in the intestine by the peristaltic movement.

Chyme is a thick semifluid mass of partially digested food and digestive secretions that is expelled by the stomach into the duodenum.

Peristalsis is a propulsive movement, which consists of a segment of contraction behind and relaxation in front.

Segmentation consists of a segment of bowel contracting at both ends, and then a second contraction occurs in the center of the segment to force the chyme both backward and forward. It is the small intestine's primary method of motility during digestion of a meal.

Migrating motor complexes (MMC) are the peristaltic motor patterns that occur during fasting. They migrate from the stomach to the distal ileum.

Haustrations are the characteristic saclike segments seen in the large intestine.
emphasis: Peristaltic contractions propel chyme aborally through the small intestine

rationales.a: Segmentation primarily mixes chyme rather than propelling it long distances.
rationales.b: Haustration is colonic mixing, not small-intestinal propulsion.
rationales.c: Migrating motor complexes occur during fasting between meals.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q006.takeaway: Local distension of the gut wall is the major initiating stimulus for the peristaltic reflex.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q006.displayText:
Local distension of the gut wall is the major initiating stimulus for the peristaltic reflex.

The major initiating response for peristalsis is local stretching of the gut.

Peristalsis is a reflex response that is initiated when the gut wall is stretched by the contents of the lumen. It occurs in all parts of the gastrointestinal tract from the esophagus to the rectum.

The stretch initiates a circular contraction behind the stimulus and an area of relaxation in front of it. The wave of contraction then moves in an oral-to-caudal direction. This propels the contents of the lumen forward at rates that vary from 2 to 25 cm/s.
emphasis: Local distension of the gut wall is the major initiating stimulus for the peristaltic reflex

rationales.a: Hormones can modify motility but local stretch initiates the reflex.
rationales.c: Enteric neural circuits mediate the reflex after stretch, but are activated by local distension.
rationales.d: Gastric acid is not the primary local trigger for intestinal peristalsis.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q007.takeaway: Parasympathetic stimulation generally increases GI motility and peristalsis.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q007.displayText:
Parasympathetic stimulation generally increases GI motility and peristalsis.

Parasympathetic stimulation results in increased peristalsis.

Generally, the stimulation of parasympathetic nerves (PNS) causes an increase in the activity of the entire enteric nervous system. This, in turn, enhances the activity of most gastrointestinal functions.

PNS stimulation causes:
• Contraction of smooth muscle in the wall
• Relaxation of sphincters
• Increased salivary secretion
• Increased gastric secretion
• Increased pancreatic secretion

SNS stimulation causes:
• Relaxation of smooth muscle in the wall
• Contraction of sphincters
emphasis: Parasympathetic stimulation generally increases GI motility and peristalsis

rationales.a: Parasympathetic activity promotes gallbladder contraction rather than sphincter closure as the general response.
rationales.c: Decreased motility is a sympathetic effect, not parasympathetic.
rationales.d: Parasympathetic activity stimulates, rather than decreases, exocrine pancreatic secretion.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q008.takeaway: VIP mediates relaxation ahead of a peristaltic bolus (ascending/anterograde relaxation) through enteric inhibitory neurons.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q008.displayText:
VIP mediates relaxation ahead of a peristaltic bolus (ascending/anterograde relaxation) through enteric inhibitory neurons.

VIP is responsible for anterograde dilatation of the small intestine.

Peristalsis involves the contraction of a segment of intestine behind the bolus of food and relaxation of a segment of the intestine in front of the bolus of food.

Cholinergic neurons passing in anterograde direction produce NO and VIP which cause relaxation of a segment of the intestine in front of the bolus.

Cholinergic neurons passing in retrograde direction produce substance P and acetylcholine which cause contraction of a segment of the intestine behind the bolus.

Note: In achalasia cardia, there is decreased release of NO and VIP in the distal part of the esophagus.
emphasis: VIP mediates relaxation ahead of a peristaltic bolus (ascending/anterograde relaxation) through enteric inhibitory neurons

rationales.b: Acetylcholine contracts circular muscle behind the bolus.
rationales.c: Substance P contributes to contraction behind the bolus rather than relaxation ahead.
rationales.d: Serotonin helps initiate enteric reflexes but is not the main inhibitory dilator transmitter.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q009.takeaway: Substance P excites circular muscle behind the bolus, producing oral-side contraction during peristalsis.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q009.displayText:
Substance P excites circular muscle behind the bolus, producing oral-side contraction during peristalsis.

Substance P and acetylcholine are released from neurons behind the bolus of food, causing smooth muscle contraction, which propels the food downwards.

NO and VIP are released by neurons in the anterograde direction from the bolus which produces relaxation in front of the stimulus.
emphasis: Substance P excites circular muscle behind the bolus, producing oral-side contraction during peristalsis

rationales.a: Nitric oxide relaxes smooth muscle ahead of the bolus.
rationales.b: VIP relaxes muscle ahead of the bolus.
rationales.c: Serotonin helps activate sensory/enteric pathways but is not the final excitatory motor transmitter here.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q010.takeaway: Enkephalin inhibits gastric motility; substance P and tachykinins such as substance K promote it.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q010.displayText:
Enkephalin inhibits gastric motility; substance P and tachykinins such as substance K promote it.

Encephalin inhibits the motility of the stomach.

ECL: enterochromaffin-like.
emphasis: Enkephalin inhibits gastric motility; substance P and tachykinins such as substance K promote it

rationales.b: Angiotensin is not the keyed inhibitory enteric transmitter.
rationales.c: Substance P stimulates smooth-muscle contraction and motility.
rationales.d: Substance K is an excitatory tachykinin in GI motility.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q011.takeaway: Enteric neural reflexes coordinate gastric emptying, integrating antral activity and pyloric resistance.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q011.displayText:
Enteric neural reflexes coordinate gastric emptying, integrating antral activity and pyloric resistance.

Gastric emptying is mainly regulated by enteric reflexes.

Regulation of gastric emptying is mainly by the inhibitory feedback signals from the duodenum that includes enterogastric reflex and hormonal feedback by cholecystokinin.

Enterogastric reflex: When food enters the duodenum, multiple nervous reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall. They strongly inhibit the pyloric pump propulsive contractions and increase the tone of the pyloric sphincter.

These reflexes are mediated by three routes:
• Directly from the duodenum to the stomach through the enteric nervous system in the gut wall (major role)
• Through inhibitory sympathetic nerve fibers to the stomach (minor role)
• Vagus nerves to the brain stem where they inhibit the normal excitatory signals transmitted to the stomach (minor role)

Hormonal feedback: Cholecystokinin is released from the mucosa of the jejunum in response to fatty substances in the chyme. This hormone acts as an inhibitor to block increased stomach motility caused by gastrin.
emphasis: Enteric neural reflexes coordinate gastric emptying, integrating antral activity and pyloric resistance

rationales.a: Extrinsic neural input modulates emptying but local enteric circuits are the principal coordinating mechanism in this item.
rationales.c: Gastric hormones modify motility but are not the sole primary regulator.
rationales.d: Duodenal hormones can inhibit emptying, but the listed principal mechanism is enteric reflex control.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q012.takeaway: Gastric distension activates vagovagal and enteric reflexes that increase antral motility and gastric emptying.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q012.displayText:
Gastric distension activates vagovagal and enteric reflexes that increase antral motility and gastric emptying.

The distension of the stomach increases gastric emptying.

Distension activates the mechanoreceptors that trigger long and short reflexes in the stomach. This increases the force of antral contraction and gastric emptying.
emphasis: Gastric distension activates vagovagal and enteric reflexes that increase antral motility and gastric emptying

rationales.a: Secretin inhibits gastric emptying when acid enters the duodenum.
rationales.b: CCK slows emptying in response to fat/protein in small intestine.
rationales.c: GIP inhibits gastric activity and delays emptying.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q013.takeaway: Gastrin supports gastric motility and does not delay emptying; duodenal fat, acid and secretin slow it.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q013.displayText:
Gastrin supports gastric motility and does not delay emptying; duodenal fat, acid and secretin slow it.

Gastrin increases gastric emptying. It does not delay it.

Gastrin has mild to moderate stimulatory effects on motor functions in the body of the stomach. Thus, gastrin likely promotes stomach emptying.
emphasis: Gastrin supports gastric motility and does not delay emptying; duodenal fat, acid and secretin slow it

rationales.a: Fat in duodenum releases CCK and delays gastric emptying.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q014.takeaway: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum activates the enterogastric reflex and slows gastric emptying.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q014.displayText:
Acidic chyme entering the duodenum activates the enterogastric reflex and slows gastric emptying.

In the enterogastric reflex, gastric emptying is delayed when acidic content enters the duodenum.

When the food enters the duodenum, multiple reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall which pass back to the stomach. These reflexes slow or stop the stomach emptying if the volume of the chyme in the duodenum becomes too much. These reflexes are called enterogastric reflexes.

This reflex can be triggered due to the following reasons:
• Presence of irritants and acids in duodenal chyme (most sensitive factor)
• Distension of duodenum due to the presence of an excessive volume of chyme
• Rapid entry of hypertonic or hypotonic fluids into the duodenum
• Presence of breakdown products of protein digestion and sometimes fat
emphasis: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum activates the enterogastric reflex and slows gastric emptying

rationales.a: Gastrocolic reflex increases colonic motility after a meal.
rationales.b: Enterocolic reflex links small intestine to colon, not stomach emptying.
rationales.c: Gastroileal reflex increases ileal activity and relaxes the ileocecal sphincter.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q015.takeaway: Alkaline small-intestinal contents do not trigger the enterogastric inhibitory reflex; distension, hyperosmolarity and irritation do.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q015.displayText:
Alkaline small-intestinal contents do not trigger the enterogastric inhibitory reflex; distension, hyperosmolarity and irritation do.

Enterogastric inhibitory reflexes are stimulated by acidic contents, not alkaline.

The duodenal factors that can initiate enterogastric inhibitory reflexes (enterogastric reflexes) are:
• Distention of the duodenum
• Presence of any irritation of the duodenal mucosa
• Acidity of the duodenal chyme
• Osmolality of the chyme: either hypotonic or hypertonic fluid initiate enterogastric inhibitory reflexes. Thus, the flow of non-isotonic fluids into the small intestine is regulated. This prevents rapid changes in electrolyte concentrations in the extracellular fluid during the absorption of the intestinal contents.
• Presence of certain breakdown products in the chyme, especially proteins and to a lesser extent, of fats
emphasis: Alkaline small-intestinal contents do not trigger the enterogastric inhibitory reflex; distension, hyperosmolarity and irritation do

rationales.b: Hyperosmolar chyme activates duodenal feedback that delays gastric emptying.
rationales.c: Duodenal distension stimulates inhibitory enterogastric reflexes.
rationales.d: Mucosal irritation in duodenum suppresses gastric emptying.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q016.takeaway: The gastrocolic reflex increases colonic mass movements after stomach filling and meals, explaining postprandial defecation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q016.displayText:
The gastrocolic reflex increases colonic mass movements after stomach filling and meals, explaining postprandial defecation.

The cause of colonic contraction in the given situation is due to gastrocolic reflex.

Distension of the stomach by food initiates contractions of the rectum and frequently, a desire to defecate. This response is called the gastrocolic reflex. Because of this response, defecation after meals is common in children. This response may be amplified by the action of gastrin on the colon.
emphasis: The gastrocolic reflex increases colonic mass movements after stomach filling and meals, explaining postprandial defecation

rationales.a: Gastroileal reflex increases ileal peristalsis and relaxes the ileocecal valve.
rationales.b: Enterogastric reflex inhibits gastric emptying in response to duodenal contents.
rationales.c: CCK is not the primary reflex causing post-meal colonic contraction.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q017.takeaway: The diagram depicts the migrating motor complex, a fasting-state motility wave that clears residual contents.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q017.displayText:
The diagram depicts the migrating motor complex, a fasting-state motility wave that clears residual contents.

The given image shows the migrating motor complex.

The image shows 3 phases:
• Phase I - quiescent period
• Phase II - period of irregular electrical & mechanical activity
• Phase III - ends with bursts of regular activity

This occurs during the inter-digestive period at intervals of about 100 min and passes in the aboral direction at the rate of 5 cm/min. Its main function is to clear intestinal contents and prepare for the next meal.

Option A: Peristalsis is a propulsive movement, which consists of a segment of contraction behind and relaxation in front.

Option B: Segmentation and mixing help in mixing intestinal contents with digestive juices and provides time for digestion and absorption. It consists of a segment of bowel contracting at both ends, and then a second contraction occurs in the center of the segment to force the chyme backward and forward.

Option D: Basal Electrical Rhythm is fluctuation in the resting membrane potential of smooth muscle cells of the intestine as shown in the source.
emphasis: The diagram depicts the migrating motor complex, a fasting-state motility wave that clears residual contents

rationales.a: Peristalsis is a local fed-state propulsion wave rather than a recurring fasting interdigestive cycle.
rationales.b: Segmentation consists of stationary mixing contractions.
rationales.d: Basic electrical rhythm denotes slow waves, not the migrating motor pattern.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q018.takeaway: The migrating motor complex travels roughly 5 cm/min and recurs about every 100 minutes during fasting.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH33_Q018.displayText:
The migrating motor complex travels roughly 5 cm/min and recurs about every 100 minutes during fasting.

Migrating motor complex (MMC) migrates from the stomach to the distal ileum at a rate of about 5 cm/min and also occurs at intervals of approximately 100 minutes.

MMC is a type of gastrointestinal motility that occurs during fasting between periods of digestion. It is initiated by motilin. It helps to clear the stomach and small intestine of luminal contents in preparation for the next meal. Gastric secretion, bile flow, and pancreatic secretion increase during each MMC.

After ingestion of a meal, secretion of motilin is suppressed and the MMC is abolished.

Each cycle of MMC has 3 phases:
• Phase I - quiescent period
• Phase II - period of irregular electrical & mechanical activity
• Phase III - ends with bursts of regular activity

Note: Disorders of MMC have been associated with gastroparesis, intestinal pseudo-obstruction, and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.
emphasis: The migrating motor complex travels roughly 5 cm/min and recurs about every 100 minutes during fasting

rationales.a: 90 cm/min and a 5-minute interval are too fast and frequent for MMC.
rationales.c: 5 cm/min is the velocity, but 90 cm/sec/5 min is not the MMC interval.
rationales.d: 5 cm/sec is much faster than the slow migrating complex.
